profile.address: 1010, Boolean Drive, Clarksville, Montgomery County, Middle Tennessee, Tennessee, 38040
profile.reading:
Google's Montgomery County data center sits outside Clarksville, Tennessee, on roughly 1,300 acres originally assembled for a Hemlock Semiconductor polysilicon plant that Hemlock cancelled before it ever operated, leaving the site and much of its industrial infrastructure available for reuse. Tennessee's governor and state economic-development office announced in December 2015 that Google had chosen the site for a new data center, citing the state's reliable energy infrastructure, skilled workforce, and business climate; local officials at the time noted that data-processing employment in the Clarksville area had grown 305 percent over the preceding five years. Google broke ground on February 16, 2018, with a stated $600 million initial investment, a projected at-least-70 permanent jobs once operating, and a construction workforce of 1,000 or more during the build -- part of a concurrent $2.5 billion, 14-state Google infrastructure expansion announced that year that also included the company's Jackson County, Alabama campus. The facility opened for operation in 2019, becoming, at announcement, Google's eighth U.S. and 15th global data center.

Google structured its Tennessee Valley Authority power arrangement so the Clarksville site's consumption would be matched by renewable energy procurement, and the company committed to scouting new renewable generation projects to add to the regional grid. At groundbreaking, Google pledged $300,000 to Goodwill Industries of Middle Tennessee and funded 100 technology-education scholarships for area students.

Google's public materials describe far larger, statewide commitments tied to its overall Tennessee presence -- more than $6 billion invested in the state since 2018, more than $20 million in philanthropic giving since 2006, digital-skills training for over 192,000 Tennesseans, and coaching for more than 6,000 small businesses through its Grow with Google and Tennessee Digital Coach programs -- though these figures describe Google's statewide footprint, including other Tennessee facilities and offices, rather than the Clarksville site alone. Google's Tennessee location materials also cite a partnership with Kairos Power and TVA on an advanced nuclear reactor project as part of the company's regional power strategy, though that reactor work is centered elsewhere in Tennessee rather than at this facility.

As with Google's other data centers, the company does not publish IT capacity in megawatts, floor area, or server-hall configuration for this specific building.

reading.body:
This campus has no published power specifications in the operator's documentation reviewed by this site. The address places it in Clarksville, Montgomery County, Tennessee, within Google's documented data center footprint in the region, but individual megawatt capacity for this specific facility has not been disclosed. It appears in OpenStreetMap records as a mapped location.

Tennessee has 24 mapped data center facilities across the state, of which only 4 have published power figures totaling 12.13 MW. This campus ranks fifth by published capacity in the state, which indicates it either hosts published capacity not yet recovered or operates without a disclosed specification.

Without published specifications, the significance of this campus to AI infrastructure cannot be assessed from data this site holds. The operator's broader program in the Southeast is documented elsewhere, but this particular facility's capability remains opaque.
